utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Hedaraly, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you were asked questions yesterday about the St. Vitus Day parade in June 1995, I believe, end of June 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And some of the weapons on display then came from Republika Srpska and were sent there back after the parade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 7250, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you're going to see on your screen, two pictures, two photographs, of yourself that were part of the series of photographs that you had provided to the Office of the Prosecutor when you gave your statement. The first one is referenced at paragraph 8 -- picture number 18 at page 35 of your statement, and you said, This is a French captain who spoke fluent Serbian. His parents were Serbs, but he was born in France, and you state that you are there wearing a British uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that is at paragraph -- well, item number 78 at page 40 of your statement. This time you're there in a French uniform on the day the RSK army gave its first pledge at Petrova Gora to a nobody. I just want to ask you, why were you wearing different uniforms, a French uniform, a British uniform, what was the idea behind this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vanity. I look good in it. But if you look at both photographs, you'll find out that the British uniform and the French uniform carry the insignia of the RSK on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And is that something that you would do regularly in the course of your assignments or when you would meet with people to wear uniforms of different nationalities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- with me it was on a regular basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what other uniforms would you wear?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a Polish uniform, I had a Dutch uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you wear all of these on a regular basis. Would you just -- whatever you felt like in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Switch them around, yes, whichever was clean the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a JNA uniform, too, but it looked ridiculous. Ah, the vanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to briefly talk to you about the four peace conferences that you attended. And now there were tow in Geneva, one in Vienna, one in Norway; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The first one was on 16 June 1993 in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume you have the right date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm relying on your testimony in the Milosevic case --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just for the record, it's at 12401, lines 22 to 25 there. And the next one was on -- all of these are from the transcript in Milosevic, just so I tell you what I'm relying on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Because then I had actual passport in front of me, so I read the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And yet you testified yesterday that everything that you testified to in Milosevic was the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So the next one was on 16 July 1993 in Geneva. Then shortly thereafter, 20 to 22nd July, 1993, in Vienna, and the last one was 12th September, 1993, in Norway. Is that generally also consistent with your memory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, references to the Milosevic transcript would be accompanied by an observation, if they were not in evidence from what I -- not to say that it's illegal to do that, but the reference you just made is to a portion which is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour, I don't need to tender it. I simply want the dates to be here, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... No, no. I'm not inviting you, but just for us to know whether we can verify it, yes or not, in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, it is not in the evidence, those portions. I can refer to each of the references to each of the dates, but since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that if there are any problems with that that we would hear from the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So the first one, 16 June, the last was 12th September, 1993. So when you testified about these negotiations between the RSK and Croatia, these are meetings and events surrounding these meetings that you attended; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that's in the period of roughly three months, June to September?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And by the time Operation Storm started, it had been roughly two years since had you attended a peace negotiation; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you are not aware of any details about the negotiations in Geneva on the 3rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You don't --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I wasn't part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was just pausing because of the translation. I was not suggesting that your answer was not complete.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you don't know -- you didn't know at the time the details of what was negotiated, who accepted what, or who refused what, and so on; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, if I can tender 65 ter 7250, and I will then complete -- that will conclude my cross-examination, the two photographs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2535 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lazarevic, there are two matters I'd like to briefly address. The first is the lapse of time between you were informed about the attack by Mr. Jenssen and the commencement of the attack. In the Milosevic case, you testified, and I will read it to you: "The operation itself started on the morning of August the 5th," which, at least the parties here say it's the 4th, "however, we have been inferred about a pending attack two days prior in every detail about the time, the strength, and the direction of the attack." And you then said you learned this through your connections with ECMM. Mr. Misetic, where you said that the name of Mr. Bent Jenssen was mentioned in the Milosevic trial on that page, it's not, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is in the statement, though, which is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but Mr. Misetic specifically said, we find -- but let's try to focus on my question. Yesterday you testified that it was the day before the attack that you learned about it, not two days prior to the attack. Now, which one is the correct version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had enough time to read my statements at a later stage and kind of go through my memory, and it was absolutely the day before the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So what you said in your statement and your testimony here in court overrules what you said as a witness in the Milosevic trial. You -- that then was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my memory then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And obviously I made a mistake. It was done willingly. I mean, no ulterior motives to it. I would like to remind Your Honour that there were five days of my life which are absolutely terrifying and confusing at the time. Making a mistake of, did it happen early afternoon or early morning next today, to me, is one and the same, for simple reason, I only remember being day or night. I don't remember the dates anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I'm not -- it's just you attested to both -- to your statement and to the transcript, so, therefore, I consider that important to establish what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. I thought [indiscernible] was present when Jenssen was giving that information me. And she is absolutely certain it was the day before the attack which confirmed my doubts maybe I have the wrong date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Now finally the Chamber was a bit confused about the testimony about what was played, and what was not played, and what instilled fear, what tapes were played. Let me take you back to a part of what you told us today. You told about -- I think about tapes from a Croatian origin where you said: "These tapes are made prior to conflict, you're correct, so I have not seen any tapes made after the actual conflict had started." And then a question was put to you: "And they were not made but they were played during the conflict." And then you said: "They were played, yes." Now, later in your testimony you said that you had no electricity and you couldn't watch television at all. That's a bit -- a puzzle for me, where, on the one hand, you said they were played, and they were made prior to the conflict; they were played also after the conflict had started. But you're unable to watch television. Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a period of time in RSK where we did not have power. We got power about 18 months after I arrived on the ground. So anything that happened in those 18 months, it was televised or placed on radio, I have no idea or knowledge because I just couldn't see it. After that period, once we got the TV back -- and it was mostly the HRT, it wasn't a Yugoslav television --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you tell me exactly what point in time you are talking about when you got the electricity back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came in -- I came in in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the UN came in early 1992, so it would be halfway down the road, so, let's say, June/July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you were referring to the conflict, you were referring to, you said not seen any tapes made after the actual conflict has started. Are you talking about Operation Storm or the conflict in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the conflict in its entirety. So I'm covering the period of time that I was this Topusko, from 1991 to August 1995. For the first 18 months of that period, we did not have electricity. Eighteen months later, yes, we did. In that entire period of time, there were no Croatian tapes played on the TV that I have seen. But I did see tapes which are kind of reruns of the things that happened prior to the conflict, the Spegelj tapes, for example, they were made much earlier than when the conflict happened. And the ones which I have seen that were made later than the conflict would be the Medak pocket tapes, which were televised on Canadian television, somebody got a tape out and gave it to us, so we played it on our television as well. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let me try to understand the gist of your answers given to Mr. Hedaraly also in relation to your statement and your testimony earlier. Did I understand you well when you said that both from the Serb side and from the Croatian side there was broadcasts, television, which, from both sides, depicted the situation you could expect, which was not a good one, so that both the Serb side and the Croatian side, whether we call it propaganda, not, but at least televised programmes which were of a kind that you could get scared about what would happen once the Croats would be in power again? Is that well understood or not? Please correct me if I'm wrong. I'm trying to understand the gist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a distinction here. I don't think I have ever said that the Croatian or the Serbian side had a programme on the TV in relation to what will happen if Krajina falls. That would be from the Serbian side, not the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So everything they had it on a tape from Croatian parliament, it was chosen to be shown on Banja Luka TV, so we can see it. And that would be the one that we can -- didn't feel too good about it. So it was a selective programming from the Serbian TV, not the Croatian TV. It might have happened in Croatia at certain period of time and they would take out of context and screen it for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So Serbian TV depicted a situation of horror, suggesting that this is what you could expect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas the Croatian television you said showed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't watch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't watch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. So it came from one side only. But you said a second ago, let me just ... The Serbs would show what happened in Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was entirely from the Serb side that the public was informed about the disastrous events that one could expect once the Croats would be in power again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to make it more clear, there was a live broadcast on Croatian TV, sitting of a parliament. And you got this guy coming up with the Ustasha salute. It would be taken over by Serbian, made into short film, and shown on our TV, not the whole sitting of the parliament all day long, just this session. And they would kind of reinforce what they are saying, that nothing good would come out of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was mainly because they selected those portions, whereas, although you didn't watch Croatian television, that if you would have watched it, it would have just been a moment and not focussed propaganda but just a moment in parliamentary events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I wanted to verify whether I understood, and I apparently did not understand your testimony well, so that's -- that was a good exercise. Thank you for those answers. Any need to put further questions to Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you were asked about what happened when you got to Serbia and people being directed to Kosovo. Let me just ask you, obviously you testified in the Milosevic trial. Are you aware of the testimony of Milan Babic on the same point that you were making, regarding direction of Krajina Serb refugees to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is at -- we've tendered this as 92 quater testimony of Mr. Babic and is, for the record, transcript page 13263 to 64 in the Milosevic trial. And it is Mr. Babic's conversation with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think -- I think that is quite leading, and it is also a matter of -- the point that I made was that he didn't have any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- I heard one question, are you aware of the testimony of Milan Babic? And then in a rather -- the reference to the content of it is, I would say, relatively neutral. The answer was, No, I'm not aware of it. Now Mr. Misetic says, just for the Court's information, this is where I refer to. I didn't hear any further question -- I don't know whether there's any question following, so leading here ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, to the extent he is going to read something that the witness is not aware of and then ask him then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Misetic is going to read it. He did not announce that -- yes -- yet. Do you want to read that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, I will not read it, if he doesn't know anything it. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I expected, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- I'm a limited confused because Mr. Hedaraly says he only asked him what he knew about it. I don't know -- I assume from his questioning on that point that this is now a point in dispute between the Defence and the Prosecution. And I wish to point out the position of the Prosecution in the Milosevic case on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, should we do that in the presence of the witness, or should we do that at an -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Hence why I was going to move on and not put anymore questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I expected you would do, but Mr. Hedaraly has apparently some other expectations. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly will be happy, and you do what you intended to do anyhow. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you were asked a few questions about the interpreters and whether they could affect the reporting of the ECMM and the UN. And I wanted to bring you back to page 10 of your 1999 statement. And if I could hand you again a copy of your 1999 statement. It's page 10 at the top. You say: "Our sole objective was to obstruct the work of the ECMM, and later of the UN. We did everything to keep them from finding out the truth, and we repeatedly supplied them with misinformation. It was amazing to us how often they believed what we were saying. But if you keep repeating the same lies again and again, it seems as if anyone would eventually conclude that it must be true, that no one could lie so often and so consistently." My question to you is: When you were supplying them with misinformation, was it your intent that they report that misinformation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if in fact the UN and the ECMM would then report your misinformation on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any -- did you ever encounter a situation where they contested or disputed the misinformation you were giving them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I ever contested it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, that you provided them misinformation, and they challenged your account?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what would happen in those instances?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they wouldn't use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In instances where they didn't challenge the misinformation that you had provided them, what would you assume?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they would use it to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked about the information that Mr. Jenssen had provided you, and you said that it was information about the attack in Sector North. Yet you provided that information to the Knin HQ. Why did you forward information about an attack in Sector North to the Knin HQ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military structure requested it. This is your HQ. This is my army. My sector is going to be attacked. My commanding officer is sound asleep. I'm sending it to the HQ instead of him sending. But HQ need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. On this issue of the Spegelj tapes, you had indicated to Mr. Hedaraly that they were produced by the JNA. Can you explain what you know about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really place the date. It was absolutely before the conflict. I think Slovenia was still in -- in Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The military section of KOS had followed Spegelj and made some secret tapes of his meetings, and I think it was screened on the Croatian TV as well. So it was not something that was done in Belgrade and just for benefit of Belgrade. It was done for the benefit of all of Yugoslavia at the time. So everybody had a chance to look at it, listen it, they even had a subtitle in the case you missed what was said. But if I to put a date on it, I would say at least a year before anything really bad happened in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the Croatian position was on the authenticity of that KOS tape?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They argued a point that it's all made up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But whoever -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you very much, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, this concludes your evidence in this court, unless Mr. Hedaraly would --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was just wondering whether we should let the witness finish his last answer as he started saying a few words and then was stopped. I was struggling with his last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you would like to know the whole of his answer. Mr. Lazarevic, I'll read to you what is on the transcript as last question and answer. The question was: "Do you know what the Croatian position was on the authenticity of that KOS tape? You then said: "They argued a point that it's all made up," that it was all made up, I understand. And then you continued to say: "But whoever ..." and then you were stopped. What did you want to add to the answer you gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody else thought they are the genuine tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it was only the Croatians who thought it was a fraud, and you say others --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To us, at the time, it was no surprise that the Croatian authorities would deny that those tapes are genuine. Rest of us, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonian, Bosnia looked at it, no, it is genuine tape, kind of fits with the profile of a new budding Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for completing that answer. Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Lazarevic. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to answer the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, is the Gotovina Defence ready to call it's next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your next witness will be Ms. Vesna Skare Ozbolt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have to wait until the usher returns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Ms. Skare Ozbolt, you will first be examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. You may proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We have met and talked before. I'd like to first address the statement that you provided. And with the assistance of the usher if I could give a hard copy to the witness, I would appreciate it. And for the record this is 65 ter 1D2686.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have to ask you some questions with regard to that. Now, do you recall meeting with the members of the Gotovina Defence team on the 3rd of October, 2007, as reflected in the front of that sheet. Yes?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... signing that document --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On 13 June 2008?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as we go through this and just looking at this document can you just state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: My full name is Vesna Skare Ozbolt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just Ms. Skare Ozbolt, just looking at the statement that's before you, you have -- have you had a chance to look through that document before you came in here today?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes. And I do have a small correction to make at point 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what that correction is.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: It's the word "stablisation," under paragraph 10. The term normalisation would more accurately reflect what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the exception of this one clarification, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, would the rest of the document accurately reflect what you told the members of the Gotovina Defence team at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I asked the same questions that are detailed in that statement, would you give the same answers, with the exception of the one clarification that you made?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, at this time we'll offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2686 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1471, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1471 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did in fact discuss the summary with the witness prior to coming in here today, so she is aware of the purpose of that summary. If I may, with Your Honours permission, just read that briefly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As of 20 January 1995, Vesna Skare Ozbolt was the assistant Chief of Staff of the office of the president of the Republic of Croatia. Ms. Ozbolt participated in negotiations on behalf of the Republic of Croatia with representatives of Serb authorities in attempts to achieve the peaceful reintegration of the so-called Republic of Serb Krajina. These negotiations included negotiations in Geneva on 3 August 1995. Ms. Ozbolt will testify that Croatia's goal was always the peaceful reintegration of its sovereign territory and that had the representatives of the so-called Republic of Serb Krajina in Geneva accepted Croatia's proposal, Operation Storm would not have commenced on 4 August 1995. Rather, a peaceful reintegration would have occurred similar to the process later undertaken with the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia. Ms. Ozbolt will also testify that the fact that the United States Ambassador Peter Galbraith had obtained Milan Babic's acceptance of the Z-4 plan while the negotiations in Geneva were ongoing was irrelevant, because Dr. Babic, at that time, was in no position to implement the plan. Ms. Ozbolt will further testify that it was not Croatia's intent to remove the Serbs from the occupied territories in the Krajina and that she personally received numerous instructions to take all means to ensure that as many Serbs as possible remained in Croatia. That would be the basic summary of the testimony. With Your Honours' permission, if I could proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I understand that the summaries have no evidentiary value, but I would have taken issue with some of the characterizes of what was in that statement based on the summary, and I just want to put that on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was good practice that the summaries would be sent to the other parties to see whether there would be any objection to the way in which the statements would be summarized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that didn't happen through the entire Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I never -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I did object about it on several occasions. When summaries were given, I objected to how it was framed, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I always thought that that was in view of what was -- had been sent. Then I -- if this -- then I'm perhaps confusing the practice in other cases where we resolved these matters by inviting the parties to share the content of the summary in advance so that if there would be any problems that it could be resolved between the parties primarily, and if I'm wrong, Mr. Kehoe, then I have done great injustice to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's -- I'm just pointing out how we have been practicing to date. What we have provided, of course, and the Prosecution has provided us, and we did the same, is to the extent that there are additions, some deviations concerning what is in the 92 ter statement, we provide a supplemental sheet to counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber is aware of that the proofing notes or -- we will find another moment to see -- if this was a once incident, then, of course, we shouldn't pay too much attention to it. But if this would be a repeating issue, then of course, we would have to find a more satisfactory solution for it. Ms. Skare Ozbolt, let's move on and not waste your time, I'm not saying our time, but not waste your time with, at this moment, further exploring this matter. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, basically in your statement we are talking events that took place from 1994 and 1995 while you were working in the Croatian government. But can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of your experience beginning in 1991, your experiences and what jobs you held while you were in working for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: In 1991, I became advisor to the president of the republic for public relations, which post I held up until sometime in 1994, when, for a short period of time, I was his Chief of Staff of the office, and then, rather, chef de cabinet, and then subsequently assistant to the Chief of Staff of the office where I was charged with relations with representatives of the occupied territories in Croatia and with missions of representatives of the United Nations representation offices present in Croatia. When the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia commenced, I was on behalf of the president of the republic, charged together with the head of mission of the UN, UNTAES, Jacques-Paul Klein with the process of reintegration itself. In 1997, I held the position, which was called the president of the national committee for confidence restoration and reconciliation between the Serbs and Croats. These are all the positions I held. And in addition to these, I was advisor to the president of the republic for political matters up until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the president that you're talking about throughout all this is President Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I'm referring to the president of the republic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago that you took over the position of the assistant Chief of Staff to the president. And I'd like to show you a document that is 65 ter 1D2608.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just put that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you could take a look at this, Ms. Ozbolt.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just -- do you recognise this, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and what is it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: This is the decision appointing myself to the position of the assistant Chief of Staff of the office of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and this is 30 January 1995?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You see it's in the left -- it's the lower left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, can I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2608.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1472 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, your statement, and I'm talking specifically where you discuss in paragraphs 2, 4, and 5, you discuss your experiences concerning negotiations with the Krajina Serbs concerning the reintegration. Now, when did you first begin to negotiate with the Krajina Serbs concerning some type of resolution to the issue that was -- had formed the Republic of Serb Krajina. When did you begin?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I must admit, that the process was embarked upon far earlier. Back in 1991, as early as 1991, I visited the Knin area on two occasions and talked to the then representatives of authority there. Subsequently, in the capacity of the assistant to the Chief of Staff of the office, I negotiated, together with the Chief of Staff, the opening up of roads, particularly in the area of Western Slavonia, and at a later date, in the area of eastern -- of Eastern Slavonia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we are -- in your statement, you talk about the negotiations in 1995. And you just noted for us, there were negotiations prior to that. Throughout all these negotiations was there a -- some fundamental negotiating positions that the Republic of Croatia had with regard to the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: The negotiations were ongoing, as of 1991, and gathered pace in late 1994, when certain specific and tangible results were obtained. The so-called economic agreement was signed between Borislav Mikelic, as a representative of the so-called government of the SAO Krajina, and Hrvoje Sarinic. Thereafter, negotiations continued about the issue of opening up of roads in Western Slavonia; whereas, the agreement I referred to earlier was signed in late 1994. The objective of the agreement was to ensure that the railway lines and the highway leading from Zagreb towards Eastern Slavonia be opened up, as well as the oil pipeline traversing the area. Another goal was to ensure the opening up of the roads leading to southern Croatia. The agreement signed at the time was regarded as a very positive one, in our view. However, it did not take hold because the representatives of the SAO Krajina did not honour it. The person who signed the agreement on their side, Borislav Mikelic, experienced a great deal of trouble for having signed the agreement to begin with. The highway which was opened at the time was shut down again since it was the subject of numerous incidents. Thus, up until the commencement of Operation Flash, there were certainly around 90 incidents observed along that particular highway. When it became evident that the negotiations made no sense and once we have exhausted all our options, on the 1st of May, Operation Flash commenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take you back even before Operation Flash, and I would like to direct to you paragraph 2 in your statement, and I believe it's the fourth sentence in paragraph 2, where you say that: "The Republic of Croatia's goals in these negotiations was the peaceful reintegration of the so-called Krajina into the Republic of Croatia." Now --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. That was the goal, and that was the way by which we wanted to reintegrate not only the territory involved but also the individuals residing in the area; that's to say, the Serbs. Our goal was to restore the territory back to the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia through peaceful means, to ensure that the Serb population residing in the area stayed there and was reintegrated into the society, and to have the population that had been previously expelled from the territory return. Our intention was to embark on a -- on the process with peaceful means, since the purpose was to put a stop to all the effects that the war had inflicted on the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So correct me if I'm wrong, but peaceful reintegration, the Serbs would stay in the Krajina and the Croatian population that had been expelled after 1991 would come back.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How long in your -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. This was in fact the initial agreement that the Croatian government signed in 1992, when the first peace plan was signed, that was the Vance Plan, when the first peacekeeping forces arrived in Croatia. This was precisely the objective, to stop the war and to ensure a gradual -- a reintegration of the territory into the constitutional system of the Republic of Croatia and the reintegration of the population into Croatian society.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, you noted for us just now, I believe, that this was the first -- the peaceful reintegration was the first plan beginning in 1992. Did the plan for peaceful reintegration stay in effect up until Geneva on the 3rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: It did. However, there was a serious problem, which was that the UN peace mission did not fulfil the task it had been sent there to begin with. It did fulfil its primary task of putting a stop to hostilities, but it did not fulfil the other tasks, the second being the demilitarization of the area, and the third task being the return of the population and normalization of life. This was something that the UN failed to do through its mission there which was called UNPROFOR. Ultimately for this reason, all the steps had to be taken which were eventually taken. I would, however, like to point out that following Operation Flash that when the highway was opened, the Croatian government allowed free passage of trucks from the direction of Serbia toward Sector South; that's to say, toward the Knin area, and allowed a free flow of supplies that ensured normal life for them. Every day trucks passed along the highway that the Croatian police checked for possible weapons, and subsequently allowed them to continue their journey onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, may I invite you to take a breath every now and then, which would allow our transcribers and interpreters to take a breath every now and then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for you guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, let's take this in a little bit more chronological order. And you mentioned that UNPROFOR -- or the view of Republic of Croatia is that UNPROFOR did not complete its tasks successfully. And thereafter, after their mission stopped or was not renewed by the Republic of Croatia, another mission was signed with the Republic of Croatia and the UN called UNCRO. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: That's right. As I said, the UNPROFOR mission performed excellently at the start by stopping the war. However, its subsequent performance was that of a peacekeeper, rather than a peacemaker. It did not put into effect the demilitarization and did not ensure the return of the displaced persons. This was a serious problem, despite the fact that the Security Council resolutions which were passed in the meantime were useful for Croatia because they kept reaffirming Croatia within its state borders. However, the years went by, and the status quo remained. This was quite hard for Croatia to endure, since, at the time, Croatia was blocked and cut off into at least three parts; namely, the southern part, the direction toward Dalmatia, where the area around Knin was occupied, made it impossible for that region to function at all. Likewise, the eastern part of Croatia was severed from the central part of the country. In economic terms, Croatia was unable to function this way in the long-term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... stop you right there. And let's see if we can take some of these issues, and we'll get into these issues that you're talking about as we go through some of documents. Now you noted that UNPROFOR then became UNCRO. And this was the latter part of 1994, going into the earlier part of 1995, was it not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during -- when they moved -- when Croatia moved from UNPROFOR to UNCRO, did the position of the Republic of Croatia for negotiating through a peaceful reintegration of the RSK, did that change, when they went from --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: No, no. This never changed. It remained the same. The only thing that changed were international representatives, with whom we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a presidential transcript for a meeting held at the palace that you attended on 11 January 1995, and that would be 65 ter 1D261 -- excuse me, 1D2613. Let me just show the cover page first and then we can turn to individual pages. Just scroll that down. As you can see this is 11 January 1995. You are present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to turn to page 14 in the English, and I do believe it's the same page in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is a discussion of a letter that goes on at some length that discusses the transition from -- from UNPROFOR to UNCRO, and it lays out this correspondence going to the Security Council and the Secretary-General by the Republic of Croatia, and they're reading through this letter. And if we can turn to the paragraph beginning -- the first full paragraph, beginning with: "Croatia showed ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is, I do believe it's the president speaking at this time, President Tudjman, he is speaking at this time. He notes that reading this letter: "Croatia showed and proved the highest degree of the goodwill, wish for cooperation, and self-control in the last two, for us, very difficult years. Croatia even accepted significant changes of the Vance Plan, for example, about the establishment of the pink zones and blue lines. The latter ones are part of the Zagreb cease-fire agreement from 28 March -- from the 28 March, which has been violated severely. The most obviously by the coordinated offensive and aggression on Bihac by the Serbs from the occupied Croatian areas. The economical" -- should be economic, of course. "The economical agreement was signed on 2 December 1994, and it should be seen as another obvious example of Croatia's readiness to accept the process of peaceful reintegration of the occupied areas." Now we refer there, Ms. Ozbolt, to the economic agreement of 2 December 1994. Is that the agreement that you were discussing previously?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the agreement that I referred to in my opening statement here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that agreement was the discussion about opening roads, railways, and other transit routes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: That's right. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And economically, at this juncture, why was that so important to the Republic of Croatia, the opening of roads, railways and highways?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: That was extremely important for the Republic of Croatia because, practically, Croatia was unable to function as a whole. The southern part of Dalmatia was completely cut off from Croatia, for example, the area of Dubrovnik and Split were totally severed. The communications were extremely difficult to maintain. The eastern part of Croatia, from Osijek onwards was totally occupied and integrated into Yugoslavia. To put it simply, that was a bread basket. However, there was no agricultural activity there. In economic terms, Croatia was stagnating and could not develop in a normal way. This agreement was extremely important. You have to know that at that time Croatia had about half a million of its own refugees who had been expelled from the occupied areas, from the Knin area and Eastern Slavonia. It had also had more than 300.000 refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina that they took care of on a daily basis. So put together, that amounted to more than 800.000 people to be supported by four and a half a million inhabitants of Croatia. That was absolutely and completely difficult to sustain, and precisely the initiative to conclude this economic agreement that would lead to opening up of roads and other communication lines was of pivotal important for Croatia. And I have to admit that we imagined that things would improved after the signing of this economic agreement. However, this never materialised because, as I said, the signatory no economic agreement, immediately after he had signed it, was removed from the office. I'm talking about Borislav Mikelic, the prime minister of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This was the prime minister of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So let us continue with this transcript, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 16 of this transcript, and we're not going read the whole thing, because it is quite extensive. But if we could just highlight a few points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, before we do that, could you find somewhere in the next five, up to ten minutes, a moment suitable for a break, because you apparently want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is as good as time as any, if Your Honour wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is it as good a time as any. Then we will have a break and resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm also looking at Mr. Misetic, who, during the last break had forgotten something which he may not have forgotten this break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He probably did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know him better. Any news?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, this time I remembered. Mr. Hedaraly and I have spoken, and in principle, the -- based on the information I relayed to him which we received from VWU, the Prosecution doesn't have any objection. Obviously there is a subpoena issue here as well, so we're trying to work out the timing with the Registrar to see when is the earliest opportunity we could get to do a videolink with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But we will file a motion seeking a videolink with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber will then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just to put on the record that it is correct that we would not object a motion for videolink for that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Misetic says so, Mr. Hedaraly, then you can refrain from seeking confirmation, but for completeness sake, it's good that you confirm it. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed. The Chamber, during the break, wondered whether you could guide the witness to find the appropriate level of detail of what is not exactly the core of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, if we can stay with this transcript of this meeting on the 11th of January of 1995 and turn to page 16, and just one last matter on this. Now I believe it is page 16 in the B/C/S version as well. Should be about two pages up. That's right. Yeah. If we can direct our attention to the bottom of the English version. And I believe it's probably -- I'm not sure where it is on the B/C/S, but nevertheless, again the president reading the letter saying: "Your Excellency, the expiration of UNPROFOR's mandate does not mean the end of negotiations. On the contrary, it should give new incentive for successful completion. The Republic of Croatia stays faithful to its peaceful politics and the peaceful reintegration of its territories. And it still offers to all Serbs ... a cultural autonomy and the highest degree of local autonomy in those districts where Serbs are a majority, according to the population census before the war." Ms. Ozbolt, just briefly, could you -- I'm going to direct you to two issues in that, and -- on that quote, and one, is the cultural autonomy and -- for Serbs as well as -- and two is the highest degree of local autonomy in those districts where Serbs were a majority before the war. Briefly, can you explain what that means for the purposes of this discussion?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: It means what the government of the Republic of Croatia, way back in 1991, and the Croatian parliament adopted, and that was the constitutional law on the rights of national minorities, granting the Serbian ethnic community in Croatia and guaranteeing them the highest degree of cultural economy, and, as well as local autonomy, wherever the Serbs constituted a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was that part of the plan of the Republic of Croatia for peaceful reintegration?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Of course, given that this law was adopted in 1991 by the Croatian parliament, it was in force throughout the whole period, throughout the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we will to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2613.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1473.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, I want to direct your attention to the Z-4 plan. And, briefly, can you tell us what the Z-4 plan is, who presented this plan, and what was the position of the Croatian authorities and the Serb authorities with respect to the Z-4 plan?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: As far as my memory serves me, the Z-4 plan came as a proposal from the contact group, or the so-called the four ambassadors, meaning the US ambassador, the Russian ambassador, the French ambassador, and the German ambassador, including the two co-chairmen of the Geneva conference. The Z-4 plan took into consideration, or, rather, envisaged the proposal that granted an extremely high degree of rights to the Serbian ethnic community; that is to say, to the Serbs from the occupied area. It also granted them practically something that no other European practice recognised at the time. This plan was drawn up sometime in late 1994 and was presented to us thereabouts the same time to us, and that is to say, to the Croatian government and the president. It was also presented to the Serbian side as well, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was essentially this plan, that Z-4 plan contemplated that there would be a state within a state, that the Republic of Serbian Krajina would be a state within the Republic of Croatia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Well, the Z-4 plan practically allowed for a possibility for the SAO Krajina to generally become a state within a state. Why do I say that? Because it envisaged the that the SAO Krajina would have its president of the state, its prime minister, its parliament, its own currency, its own emblems, like the flag and things like that, and that was absolutely unacceptable. So, when the ambassadors brought this plan to the president's office and showed it to him, it was, indeed, I have to admit, rather shocking to us. The president did not reject the plan, but he did not accept it either. He just took note of it. We analysed it at the time to a certain extent, and apart from these, let's call them political dimensions, these propositions were totally unacceptable. There was a thesis about demilitarization of this area, which was something completely incredible and impossible to accept. It meant that the Z-4 plan envisaged for demilitarization of SAO Krajina to commence three years after the date of the signing of the -- the agreement on Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me stop --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: And that it would be completed within two years which meant, in total, within five years after the signing of Z-4 plan. That would mean that sometime in 2000 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invited Mr. Kehoe to find the right level of detail. If he interrupts you, that is not because you're not telling interesting things but because is he following the guidance of the Chamber. Would you please -- this is as you'll understand not a political debate in which you would just ignore perhaps someone interrupting you. That's for good reasons. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the plan, you said that the president took note of it. Was the Republic of Croatia willing to use the Z-4 plan as a basis for beginning negotiations or negotiating with the Serb -- or the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the president neither accepted nor rejected the plan. And had the representatives of the Krajina Serbs accepted it, that would have been a starting point for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: They rejected them straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move ahead to the time-period prior to Operation Flash and directing your attention to paragraphs 2 and 3. You continued to negotiate with the Serb authorities prior to Operation Flash, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And was the purpose of these negotiations regarding Operation Flash the reopening of the road going through that area?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes. The sole reason was the opening of the highway and the railway line along the same routes, because the road and the railway line were shut off again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted for us previously that the Serbs refused to open up that road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: More precisely, they signed this economic agreement which envisaged the opening of the, road; but within the next few months, they kept shutting it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And was it because of them shutting that road off that Operation Flash went forward in the first few days of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: That's right. That was precisely the reason, because there were ongoing incidents happening on the road, and the road was impassable and it eventually led to Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, after Operation Flash took place, was there any effort on the part of the Republic of Croatia to expel the remaining Serb population from Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: No. There was no policy directed or aimed at any kind of expulsion. At the time, we were holding talks with Veljko Dzakula the representative of Serbs, and the majority of Serbs around him remained in Western Slavonia. Part of the population did leave, however, because they quite simply did not want to live in Croatia any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if you would point to a purpose for Operation Flash, would that purpose be economic reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I just ask that question to be asked in a non-leading way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was the reason for Operation Flash economic reasons, Ms. Ozbolt, to open up that road?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That just as leading as it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was, Your Lord, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kehoe, you know that. Mr. Kehoe, Ms. Ozbolt, wanted to ask you what the purpose of Operation Flash was. That was the question he had on his mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered this several times. We solely had economic reasons on our mind. That is, to open up the road, to open up the railway line, and to establish other lines of communications towards the eastern part of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Ozbolt, you mentioned during -- or prior to the break that after Operation Flash, the Republic of Croatia allowed the Serbs to bring supplies from Eastern Slavonia into the Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: All this was happening in the aftermath of Operation Flash, and after Croatia regained full control of the road. All the traffic that travelled along this road from Serbia towards Krajina went unhindered. Croatia did nothing stop it, but we did check it for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How do you know that these trucks were checked? How do you personally know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I know about that personally because every morning I received reports on my desk about the contents of these lorries. These were detailed reports sent to me by the ministry of the interior, and, on the basis of that, I saw that a large number of lorries carrying food and other staple supplies were travelling from Serbia towards Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say "other staple supplies," what are you talking about, other than food?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Well, there were car tires, footwear, clothes, household items, also oil, fuel oil was transported. So that was more or less what these -- the cargo that these lorries carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, after Operation Flash and prior to Geneva, were there negotiations between the Republic of Croatia and international officials to continue to resolve the matter concerning the peaceful reintegration of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I have to admit, that there were talks going on, on a daily basis about how to proceed with the -- the reintegration, particularly of the area around Knin. That was very difficult at the time because one felt that there was a rift in the Krajina leadership, so, at one point in time, we really didn't know who to negotiate with. In other words, we didn't have, let's call it a moderate negotiator, such as Borislav Mikelic used to be. Milan Babic, at the time, took over the leadership of the government, but in a way, this disunity was pretty prominent among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, as we move through July, and I would like to show you a couple of letters and move towards the latter part of July prior to conference in Geneva, and I would like to show you first a letter to President Tudjman dated the 30th of July, and this is 65 ter 1D2716. And I would like to talk you to about some of these documents as we begin to move towards Geneva, or the Geneva talks on 3 August. Unfortunately, we only have this in English, I do believe. Yeah. And I do believe that the witness does in fact read English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the beliefs of Mr. Kehoe are important. But we'd rather verify with you. You read English? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can read in English, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, you are familiar with this letter, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And let us turn -- there are various locations on the second page, where the demands of the RSK are set forth. And let us review the response that was given to this letter, and that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2716.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, I'd like to turn to the actual response of the Republic of Croatia, which is 65 ter 1D2710.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, there is a Croatian -- actually the original is in Croatian. The copy that we have is in English, the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Ozbolt, as the assistant Chief of Staff, you had a hand in drafting this, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you obviously recognise the final version of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to the second page that has the president's signature.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer 65 ter 1D2710 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1475, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Registrar, if we could just go back to the first page on the bottom in paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it reads that: "Such proposals are not a basis for peaceful reintegration and do not consist of a reply to any of the conditions which I laid out during the discussions [sic] that you and I had on Saturday, 29 July 1995, when I specifically stated that the negotiations on peaceful reintegration of the Croatian Serbs from the occupied areas can commence under the following conditions ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page, please. Paragraph (a), just refusal to deal with Mr. Martic who was -- had been indicted at that point. But paragraph (b) talks about the negotiations for an oil pipeline; (c), again talking about communications, opening of all communications in the railway. And these are the economic terms that the Republic of Croatia were interested in, were they not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. These were the economic conditions that existed throughout the whole period from the economic agreement and seven months later in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... And if I can just go to the last is -- discuss the implementation of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. Now, was that part and parcel of the reintegration plans of reinstituting the constitutional order in the area?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes. I already said in my introductory note that throughout this whole period on the right of the Serbian ethnic community was binding for anyone since 1991 up to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, let's move ahead to Geneva which is the 3rd of August, 1995. You were part of the negotiation team that went to Geneva to meet with international representatives and also representatives from the Republic of Serb Krajina, is that right, and you note that during the course of your statement.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now just elaborate on this a little bit. You went to Geneva as part of a team. And how did this meeting in Geneva come about?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: The letter we looked at a moment ago was one of the things that prompted it. The letter expressed anger on the part of the Croatian authorities about the fact that the UN forces did not deploy closer to the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Croatia and Serbia, which they were bound to do under the Security Council resolution, the relevant Security Council resolution. Nevertheless, after sending this caution to Mr. Akashi, we continued engaging in negotiations and accepted the proposal by Thorvald Stoltenberg to hold negotiations in Geneva. There were representatives of the SAO Krajina there, as well as our delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who was heading up the delegation from the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I think it was General Novakovic who did. However, the person who was in charge seemed to be Mr. Prijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that would be the individual, Ilija Prijic that --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Ilija Prijic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that, then, Your Honours, that's in paragraph 4 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just going through these negotiations, when you got there, can you just explain how the negotiations with Mr. Stoltenberg took place. Were you all together? Were you in separate rooms? How did it take place? And how did it ultimately resolve?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: At the outset, we held what was called a plenary session; it was a very brief one. Thereafter, we had individual conversations, discussions, between representatives of the international community, first with our side, and then with theirs. This went on for several hours. The Croatian delegation arrived at these negotiations with one open question only: Was peaceful reintegration into the constitutional and legal order of the Republic of Croatia going to be accepted? This, because all the efforts invested on our part hitherto had fallen through simply due to the reason that the Serbian side kept refusing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ultimately, did you meet face to face with the Serbian side and pose a question to them? And, if you did, what was that question?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes. Finally we saw that as time went by, we never really got the chance of having a meeting with them and putting a question to them directly as to whether they would accept the proposal or not. I told the international representative, Mr. Stoltenberg, that the two delegations should be allowed to sit together and talk. He agreed to this proposal of mine very reluctantly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but, nevertheless, he agreed. We sat down at a table together; that's to say, the two delegations and the international mediators. We asked if they would agree to a reintegration into the Croatian territory and the Croatian state system, to which their answer was a clear no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you went to Geneva, had you and the delegation been empowered to enter a -- enter into negotiations and execute an agreement with the Krajina Serbs if they were willing to peacefully reintegrate into Croatia? Were you empowered to do that by the president and the government?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: In the earlier letter, the president himself listed all the requests we had. Had they agreed to our proposals, we would absolutely have all the necessary powers. Negotiations were supposed to continue in Knin and in Zagreb, in order to put into concrete terms the proposals that we had set forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, let me turn your attention to paragraph -- to paragraph 7 of your statement and the last sentence. "A yes in Geneva by the Serbs would have meant the implementation of the same model of peaceful reintegration as was implemented in Eastern Slavonia." What do you mean by that, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Precisely what I said. In the aftermath of Operation Storm, I was charged with the reintegration of Western Slavonia on the Croatian side. This meant the reintegration of the territory, the reintegration of the population residing there. This implied the demilitarization of the area, the return of the Croats, and, finally, reconciliation between the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we can look on -- I'm not sure if that is correct or what the translation is, but you noted that in the aftermath of Operation Storm, I was charged with the reintegration of Western Slavonia on the Croatian side. Is that correct, ma'am? It's on the screen. That's what you -- was it Western Slavonia or Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Ozbolt, if the Serbs had agreed to peaceful reintegration in Geneva, would Operation Storm have nonetheless gone forward on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: It would probably have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was issue that came forward at this time by Ambassador Galbraith, who had noted that the Z-4 plan had been accepted on some level by Milan Babic. Did that influence the position of the Republic of Croatia at any point during these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: You see, Milan Babic was in Belgrade. Between him and Milan Martic, who was the president of the SAO Krajina at the time, there were disagreements. What -- did the fact that Milan Babic agreed to the Z-4 plan mean when the Serbs in Knin rejected it? It meant nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So I take it after the rejection for the terms that you put forward with the Serbs in Geneva, the negotiations ended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was when negotiations ended. However, they resumed in the aftermath of Operation Storm, and the negotiations that were resumed at the time had to do with Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
