utterances.text: And let us just move ahead. And in paragraph 8 of your statement after you left the negotiations, your delegation called President Tudjman and advised him that the negotiations were not successful. Do you see that in paragraph 8? Actually, it's in 7 and 8. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let me just show you a series of intercepts, and I know you you were not a part of these. These are intercepts that were provided by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can just get the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They are 65 ter 1D2707. And there's a series of three intercepts one at 8.50 between Mr. Martic and Mr. Prijic, one at 1223, and one at 1442. And this is on the 3rd of August, 1995. And in the interests of time, I would just like to discuss with you the last call --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can just consult with ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the sequence, this should be page 7 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the MM is Milan Martic. Obviously the IP is Ilija Prijic. "Martic: Hi, Ico. Are you done? "Mr. Prijic: No, it's still going on. We have a big problem regarding the outcome of the situation. It is not favourable to us. I'll lay it out to you and you can ... "Martic: Yes, yes. "Prijic: It says on the basis of the ... agreement. Croatian government's delegation and the Serb representatives of the authorities in Knin. It was decided to cease all hostilities and military operations on Friday at noon. The following was decided on the basis of the agreement. 1. That the pipeline opens on May 7th -- Monday, the 7 August 1995, in accordance with the agreement of 9 December 1994. "Martic: That's it? "Prijic: That's it, unless technical reasons prevented it. A meeting on the pipeline -- meeting on the pipeline for Petrinja would be held in Pleso on August 8th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. I will go as quickly -- as slowly as possible. "Martic: That is also out of the question. "Prijic: Number 2: The meeting would be held on Friday at Venzei on August 8th [sic] in Knin to set the modes of opening and controlling the railway from Zagreb to Split via Knin. "Milan Martic: God forbid. "Third, to move towards including the political issue of Serb Krajina, basing the talks on the Z-4 plan. "Milan Martic: Neither that."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, recognising that you were not part of these telephone discussions ... Recognizing that you were not part of these telephone discussions, this discussion where all these proposals are refused, that, based on your testimony, was consistent with what you experienced in Geneva, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, this is the first time I'm seeing this, but I would certainly not have been surprised by this conversation. It in fact confirms what I have already said. You can see that Martic refused to agree to anything, including the Z-4 plan, which Babic agreed to on that same day. This goes to show that there was no will to take -- for the things to take turn for the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, Your Honour. I just -- there has been a lot of leading, I haven't objected -- I've objected once. But now that we're moving into more central matters, I ask that would be less leading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the message is clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At this time, we will offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2707.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1476.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, obviously the issue of Operation Storm did in fact take place at -- on the 4th of August, 1995. And I'm interested in your discussion that you had in the sentence in paragraph 7, where you noted that, "A yes" -- this is the last sentence again in paragraph 7 that I just referred to. "A yes in Geneva by the Serbs would have meant the implementation of the same model of peaceful reintegration as was implemented in Eastern Slavonia." Now, you also note prior in that paragraph, just one sentence above, again in paragraph 7: "During the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia, when I would receive information that the Serbs wanted to leave a certain area, I would personally go to the area in order to negotiate with them in order for them to remain in the area."

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my initial question for you on that is: Why were you going to Eastern Slavonia and encouraging the Serbs to stay?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Because I was charged with that duty, to follow the peaceful reintegration on behalf of the president of the Republic. I had a clear mandate and a clear picture of what needed to be done. There was provocation and intimidation of the Serb population in Eastern Slavonia. During such incidents, entire villages wanted to pack up and leave. In such situations, my associate for Eastern Slavonia and I would get in a car and go down there to Eastern Slavonia to talk them out of leaving and to make sure that they stayed. We wanted to dispel these perceptions of fear and we were successful in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, on 93, line 6 and 7, you note that I -- "... because I was charged with that duty to follow the peaceful reintegration on behalf of the president of the Republic." Who gave that you charge to work on the peaceful reintegration? Who assigned you to this role?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: The president of the Republic. He appointed me to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And formally what was that position that you held?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Formally, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, what was the name of the position?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Initially as an advisor to the president of the Republic, I followed the reintegration process. Then, he appointed me the president of the national committee for confidence restoration and reconciliation between the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you continued to work on the reintegration in Eastern Slavonia for a significant period of time, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, from the moment the Erdut Agreement was signed, which was in November of 1995, through to the end of the UNTAES mandate which was the 15th of January, 1998. I must admit that I continued performing these duties throughout 1999, since that job was only formally ended on the 15th of January, 1998. The duties of dealing with people and their problems continued thereafter. In other words, my duties did not end with the departure of the UNTAES.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me bring up a document which is a 65 ter 1D2605, and it's a -- notes by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for the Republic of Croatia. It is in both Croatian and English, and it is notes referring to the visit of the OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities, Mr. Max - Your Honour, you're going to have to -- I don't want to mispronounce a Dutch name. It will come up in a second - van der Stoel on 19 to 21 March 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that correct pronunciation, Mr. President? I know it's Dutch, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 95 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You know this gentleman, do you not, Ms. Ozbolt?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And I -- you are in fact -- if we can flip to paragraph 6 on page 2, your name is listed as being part of the delegation who met him. And I would like to just briefly go into a couple of matters. And when you were dealing with Mr. van der Stoel, what were you dealing? What were the negotiations about, and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I normally informed representatives of the international community of all our dealings. It was especially important to work toward the reintegration of the people. The issue of Croatia reaching its border was not the sole issue; the issue was how to approach the people and how to make sure that they stayed there and lived with others. The territory was occupied by [indiscernible] Serbs, Serbs that had -- who had lived there previously; in other words, indigenous Serbs. And then Serbs who had arrived there from the area of Knin, as well as by the Serbs who had come from Yugoslavia, or Bosnia-Herzegovina, or Republika Srpska. The issue of how to make sure that the Croats were -- would return into the area was quite a complex one. It was difficult to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'll stop you there, Ms. Ozbolt, and just say, you know, with regard to these efforts, let me just go back to this document and ask you to take -- if we can go back to the first page. And look in paragraph 3, about midway through right after the brackets, it notes that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the prior page on the English as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the paragraph that notes that -- it's in the bold: "In the reports that followed, Mr. van der Stoel very positively assessed the efforts and constructiveness of Croatian in finding the solutions for the full implementation of peaceful reintegration."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, the end of paragraph 4, on page 2. Again, quoting Mr. van der Stoel, the last sentence in paragraph 4: "In conclusion he pointed out that he believes that the Croatian government truly wants the Serbs to stay, and that is acting in accordance with international standards." Now you noted before that these are the efforts -- or that you received this mandate from President Tudjman. And then just going back to your statement, that's consistent, is it not, with paragraph 7 in the middle, or where you say towards the top, that: "President Tudjman had no intention to expel the Serbs because he knew that Croatia could not be an ethnically pure state. And according to my opinion, had the president wanted to ethnically cleanse Croatia, he would have done it during Operation Flash in Western Slavonia. I personally received numerous instructions that all means needed to be taken in order to ensure that as many Serbs as possible remained."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question is confusing, compound, and leading. I'd ask Mr. Kehoe to rephrase and break it up and ask it in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you accept that invitation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will ask you, was -- quite simply, Ms. Ozbolt, did you ever hear President Tudjman express --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure what will the question will be, but it sounds like a leading one to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How is that a leading question? Did you ever hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what follows. I'm not saying so, Ms. Ozbolt, would you please wait a while before answering the question, so that the Chamber can convince itself that it is not a leading question. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, did you ever hear President Tudjman express that he wanted to expel the Serb population from the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: No. I never heard him utter such a sentence, nor did I ever see such decisions being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, you were President Tudjman's assistant Chief of Staff. Would it have been possible or feasible for President Tudjman to have a plan to expel the Serb population from the Krajina and you not to know about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: For a question like this, I would ask that some foundation to be laid as to the nature of the relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but asking about possibilities, Mr. Kehoe, is usually a -- you can ask whether -- but what is possible and what's not is not possible, asks for a judgement rather than for facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, how many days a week did you see President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many hours a day were you working with him and working around his office?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: It's difficult to say how many hours a day. Sometimes a few hours; sometimes less; sometimes I would see him only during a working lunch. It all depended on the particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you assist President Tudjman in the execution of his orders when he was telling people in the government what they should and should not do?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- very vague question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You want to lay a foundation, there's a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just re-read the question. "Did you assist President Tudjman in the execution of his orders when he was telling people in the government what they should and should not do?" Are you asking whether the witness was involved in enforcing such orders? I must admit that the question is -- is not clear to me. But sometimes if the witness considers the question clear enough, then could you please tell us how you understand the question to be -- what you understand the question to be. If you would not be able to do that, we'll invite Mr. Kehoe to rephrase it. So could you please tell us how you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe to -- [Interpretation] Yes, maybe this question should be rephrased, given that I didn't understand it fully either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then there's too many people in this courtroom who do not understand the question. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I stand as a bad question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you help President Tudjman on a daily basis doing his work in the office?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can these questions please be asked in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we try to cut this short. I understand from your position and what is usually understood to be such a position that you had a very close working relationship with President Tudjman in which you shared a lot -- where you were informed about many, many things, if not all, he was working on. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour -- [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Concerning reintegration of Eastern Slavonia, I was really tasked with very specific tasks. We exchanged information and I also executed his decisions relating to reintegration of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, what the chances are that something was still not known to the witness is a matter of assessing the totality of the evidence. The witness could not tell us what Mr. Tudjman did not share with her because that apparently is -- seems to be the issue. You say, You would have known, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You would have known. If he had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, ask a husband about his wife or wife about a husband, who are living together the whole of the day, are sharing a lot of things, it nevertheless sometimes happens to make -- to make an assessment on whether that was the case, yes or no, depends on a lot of things. And perhaps it's -- the issue seems clear to the Chamber what your apparent position is that it is almost unmanageable that Ms. Ozbolt would not have known certain things is clear to us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that appears to be the point, where Ms. Gustafson still may have her own views on the matter. The matter is clear, and unless you have the 1000-dollar question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which finally gives us the clue to the answer would gladly hear that question. If not, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do have the question, Mr. President, so that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move somewhat back chronologically, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one simple question. I have to -- the Podunavlje area, could you tell me where that is. Because that's what Mr. Van der Stoel talks about in the end of paragraph 4 of this memo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the area in the eastern part of Croatia, in the UNTAES, or UN terminology, that was referred to as Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if I did this right. I do not think I did, but if I can offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2605.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, I'd like to take you back just a bit into September of 1995. If I could direct your attention to that time-frame. And you participated in meeting with Krajina Serbs in the UN camp in Sector South, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what was your role in going down and meeting with these individuals, and approximately when was it, in September?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: This took place sometime mid-September, if I remember correctly. I went down there at the request of Mr. Akashi to assist in clearing up or resolving the situation that occurred in the camp, which is the fact that several hundreds of Serbs barricaded themselves within the compound of that camp, and they didn't want to leave it. Some of these people were wanted by the Ministry of Justice and the Croatian courts. And a problem arose there that had to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I want to show you two letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can I bring up 1D26 -- 65 ter 1D2616.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a letter from Mr. Harston, dated 9 September 1995, and in the first sentence: "This letter going to you following the meeting between Mr. Akashi and Mr. Sarinic this morning, I understand that it was agreed that charge sheets pertaining to 35 of the people in Knin compound will be delivered shortly to the UN Sector South headquarters." If we can turn to another document which is D638, which is your response of September 11th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're going to put both of them, yeah. Because we're moving into that, Your Honour, if I could just move into evidence 65 ter 1D2616.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1478.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We believe it could be D637 already. Exhibit D637.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you counsel. If it is, it's my mistake. 637?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check that, and up to that moment not decide on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm interested in your response which is D638, which, of course, the sequence makes that perfectly logical. This is your response, and going to the second paragraph: "As a reply to your last sentence specifying that the suspects in the UNCRO camp should be delivered a charge sheet in the presence of legal counsel, we owe you a clarification of the Law of the procedure procedure of the Republic of Croatia." Going to the next paragraph, the last sentence: "The charge sheet or indictment is issued only after the investigation has been complete." Now, Ms. Ozbolt, there was a serious lack of understanding on the part of the UN staff as to how the Republic of Croatia legal system worked. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I must admit, I somewhat lost patience with Mr. Harston at that time, who failed to study the European law, and that created a problem, unnecessarily, which was later on resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: And Mr. Akashi somehow intervened and mediated in finding a resolution to this problem, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, when you went down to the camp in mid-September of 1995, did you meet with various of the Krajina Serbs that were in there, and did you talk to them about staying or leaving Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was. I want things to be completely clear. I went to the camp, because that had been agreed between Akashi, President Sarinic, and myself. So I went down there and talked to those people there. I was supposed to try and persuade them to stay, particularly the families whose male members were supposed to be taken before courts and against whom investigations were launched within the Croatian legal system. I was accompanied by the -- the assistant minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what did you tell them about remaining about Croatia, if anything?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: What did I tell them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT
utterances.text: I actually talked to each and every one of them and with their families. I told them that their safety was absolutely guaranteed in Croatia, that they should go back home, that the people who were subject to criminal proceedings would receive complete and full legal assistance, if they were not able to afford a lawyer, and if they were convicted in absentia, that the proceedings would be renewed or that the re-trials would be conducted. And I tried to dissuade them from leaving. Some of them decided immediately that they would stay; whereas, the others declared that they would remain -- would not remain under any circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock. I'm not asking whether this is a suitable moment. But this is the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us indication as --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have two brief areas, Mr. President. I should be done in half an hour tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To the extent that that runs over my time, I would beg the Court 's indulgence with some objections that were just asked to get through some of these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to make the picture complete, some repetitious --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and some level of detail would add to the explanation on why you went over the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, there's no other witness waiting from what I understand. So, therefore, it is less dramatic as it would be under other circumstances. Ms. Ozbolt, we would like to see you back tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in another courtroom, Courtroom I. But before you leave this courtroom I would like to instruct you that you should it not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether the testimony already given today, or whether the testimony still to be given tomorrow. For the parties -- Yes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but it's Courtroom III tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's Courtroom III, yes. Then the the infallible Registrar did not make a mistake. I read it wrongly, although my reading was strongly suggested by what he put down on paper, although which was not on his mind. I can inform the parties about this one exhibit. It seems to be a different version of the same document, the letter of the 9th of September. 2D03-0071 seems to the one you're referring to which has a fax cover page. And then although the fax cover page says 1 out of 2, two other pages are following, so it should be 1 out of 3. And that appears to be perhaps the letter that was sent rather than the one that was received. It looks a bit different from what I could see. Perhaps, Mr. Kehoe, you could consider whether the one version is any better than the one already in evidence. We adjourn, and we resume tomorrow, 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
